claims.claim: Spathis's text-mining comparison of four best-selling series reports that A Song of Ice and Fire lacks -ly adverbs relative to the other three series.
claims.quote: the lack of -ly adverbs in Game of Thrones

claims.claim: Spathis's key-takeaway list states that Game of Thrones contains significantly fewer -ly adverbs than the other series analysed.
Spathis's adverb finding is stated only for the -ly suffixed form of the adverb, never for adverbs as a whole class.
Spathis reports no numeric adverb rate in the article's running text; the adverb comparison is carried entirely by a chart image.
Spathis removed character names, along with very frequent words and phrases, as stopwords before ranking parts of speech.
Spathis's corpus is 3,896,568 words drawn from nineteen books by four authors.
Spathis's Automated Readability Index result places Game of Thrones at the comprehension level of 11-year-olds.
Spathis reports that Martin's most frequent colour adjectives across the series are red, white and grey.
claims.quote: Notable is the usage of colors by author

verdicts.trueWording: The best fantasy is written in the language of dreams
verdicts.note: Verbatim opening sentence of the essay body on the live georgerrmartin.com page (HTTP 200, raw HTML read). All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Reality is the strip malls of Burbank, the smokestacks of Cleveland
verdicts.note: Second body paragraph, verbatim: 'Reality is the strip malls of Burbank, the smokestacks of Cleveland, a parking garage in Newark.' The paragraph sets Fantasy against Reality throughout ('Fantasy is the towers of Minas Tirith…'), so the named-concrete-places limb holds.

verdicts.trueWording: on the road toward stagnation and self-parody
verdicts.note: Live page, raw HTML: 'I think the work has to change, that a writer who repeats himself too often is on the road toward stagnation and self-parody.' Page header confirms provenance: 'Guest of Honor Speech / Delivered at Windycon X / October 7, 1983', and the passage sits in the paragraph introducing The Armageddon Rag.

verdicts.trueWording: themes recur, a distinctive voice develops
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'All writers repeat themselves to a certain extent, of course; themes recur, a distinctive voice develops, characteristic concerns and literary motifs become discernible.' Same paragraph as index 632.

verdicts.trueWording: piece-by-piece like a jigsaw puzzle forming into place haphazardly
verdicts.note: Wayback raw id_ capture fetched (HTTP 200): 'Slowly the history is unveiled, piece-by-piece like a jigsaw puzzle forming into place haphazardly, and layers of events are formed…' — fifth paragraph, as cited. Page footer confirms 'copyright © 1999-2001 Elio M. García and Linda Antonsson'; the review carries no byline.

verdicts.trueWording: more than a few POV characters whose chapters are always divided by other POVs lying in-between
verdicts.note: Verbatim on the page. Note the framing is a negative conditional — 'If you want something written… without a huge cast of characters and more than a few POV characters whose chapters are always divided by other POVs lying in-between, then A Game of Thrones may not be for you' — so the review attributes the feature to the book by clear implication rather than by direct assertion.

verdicts.trueWording: this one is more grounded in history and reality
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'Where that great work is inspired by epic legends and myth, this one is more grounded in history and reality,' the sentence immediately after naming The Lord of the Rings. Both limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: the lack of -ly adverbs in Game of Thrones
